lab.title: Identify and snapshot your lab
lab.scenario: Establish a baseline before you change anything. In a real incident, these are the first facts you collect.

steps.text: Boot your RHEL lab VM or connect to your cloud instance. Confirm you are on the intended host.
steps.verify: Verify the hostname, operating system, and kernel are what you expect.

steps.text: Read the short and structured release files. Note the major version.
steps.verify: Both files should identify Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.x and agree on the major version.

steps.text: Check the kernel and CPU architecture.
steps.verify: uname -r prints the kernel release and uname -m prints x86_64 on a standard lab VM.
dnf --version should report dnf 4.x, confirming the RPM package stack.

steps.text: Take a hypervisor or cloud snapshot named clean-install. If you cannot snapshot, record how you would rebuild the machine.
steps.verify: You should be able to return to this exact state after a failed lab.

quiz.q: Which file gives the short, human-readable RHEL release string?
quiz.why: /etc/redhat-release is the traditional short string. /etc/os-release is the structured, cross-distribution file.

quiz.q: What is the main reason an organization chooses RHEL over a fast-moving hobby distribution?
options: It offers a predictable, supported lifecycle and certified ecosystem
quiz.why: RHEL trades speed for stability, support, certification, and a defined lifecycle — not for immutability.

quiz.q: What should you do before a networking or boot lab?
options: Take a snapshot of the clean system
Switch to the root account permanently
quiz.why: A snapshot is the fastest reliable undo. Disabling security controls first teaches the wrong habit.
